source_text: Epistula ad Constantium imperatorem ̓ΕΠΙΣΤΟΛΗ ΚΥΡΙΛΛΟΥ ἘΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΥ}1 ἹΕΡΟΣΟΛΥΜΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΚΩΝΣΤΑΝΤΙΟΝ ΤΟΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΑ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ἘΝ ΟΥΡΑΝΩ ΦΑΝΕΝΤΟΣ ΣΗΜΕΙΟΥ Βασιλεῖ θεοφιλεστάτῳ καὶ εὐσεβεστάτῳ Κωνσταντίῳ Αὐγούστῳ, Κύριλλος ὁ ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐπίσκοπος ἐν κυρίῳ χαίρειν. 1 Πρώτας ταύτας ἐξ Ἱεροσολύμων πρὸς τὴν θεοφιλῆ σου βασιλείαν ἀποστέλλω γραμμάτων ἀπαρχάς, σοί τε πρεπούσας ὑποδέξασθαι κἀμοὶ παρασχεῖν· οὐ λόγων κολακείας πεπληρωμένας, ἀλλ' ἐπουρανίων μηνυτικὰς θεοπτίας· οὐδ' εὐσυνθέτους λόγων ῥητορικὰς πιθανότητας περιεχούσας, ἀλλ' ἁγίων εὐαγγελίων προρρήσεσι διὰ τῆς τῶν πραγμάτων ἐκβάσεως μαρτυρούσας τὴν ἀλήθειαν. 2 Ἕτεροι μὲν γὰρ ἀφ' ὧν ἔχουσι τὴν τιμίαν σου πολλάκις στεφανοῦσι κεφαλήν, χρυσοκολλήτους στεφάνους λίθοις διαυγεστάτοις πεποικιλμένους προσκομίζοντες. Ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐ τοῖς ἀπὸ γῆς σε στεφανοῦμεν (τὰ γὰρ ἀπὸ γῆς δωρούμενα τέλος ἔχει τὴν γῆν)· ἀλλ' ἐπουρανίων πραγμάτων θεϊκὴν ἐνέργειαν ἐν τοῖς τῆς θεοφιλοῦς σου βασιλείας καιροῖς ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις τελεσθεῖσαν τῆς σῆς εὐσεβείας μετὰ σπουδῆς ἄγομεν εἰς γνῶσιν· οὐχ ἵνα νῦν ἐξ ἀγνοίας ἔλθῃς εἰς θεογνωσίαν (φθάνεις γὰρ καὶ ἑτέρους διδάσκων δι' ὧν εὐσεβεῖς· ἀλλ' ἵνα, ἅπερ ᾔδεις, ταῦτα καὶ βεβαιωθῇς, καὶ τὸν τῆς βασιλείας προγονικὸν ὑποδεξάμενος κλῆρον, μείζοσι θεόθεν στεφάνοις ἐπουρανίοις τετιμῆσθαι μαθών, θεῷ μὲν τῷ παμβασιλεῖ καὶ νῦν τὴν πρέπουσαν ἀποδῷς εὐχαριστίαν, μείζονος δὲ τοῦ κατ' ἐχθρῶν θάρσους πληρωθῇς, ἔργῳ τὴν σὴν βασιλείαν ἀγαπᾶσθαι πρὸς θεοῦ, δι' ὧν ἐπὶ σοῦ θαυματουργεῖ, καταλαβών. 3 Ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ τοῦ θεοφιλεστάτου καὶ τῆς μακαρίας μνήμης Κωνσταντίνου τοῦ σοῦ πατρός, τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ σταυροῦ ξύλον ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ηὕρηται, τῆς θείας χάριτος τῷ καλῶς ζητοῦντι τὴν εὐσέβειαν τῶν ἀποκεκρυμμένων ἁγίων τόπων παρασχούσης τὴν εὕρεσιν.
thought_title: First fruits of heavenly news, not flattery
orientation: Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, opens his letter to the emperor Constantius by explaining that he sends not flattering words but news of a heavenly vision.
pass_a_gloss: Letter of Cyril bishop of Jerusalem to Constantius the emperor concerning the sign that appeared in heaven. To the most God-loving and most pious emperor Constantius Augustus, Cyril the bishop in Jerusalem greets in the Lord. These first fruits of letters I send from Jerusalem to your God-loving majesty, both fitting for you to receive and for me to offer; not filled with flatteries of words, but announcing heavenly visions; not containing well-composed rhetorical persuasions of words, but bearing witness to the truth of the predictions of the holy gospels through the outcome of events. For others often crown your honored head with what they have, bringing crowns inlaid with gold and adorned with most brilliant stones. But we do not crown you with things from the earth (for things given from the earth have the earth as their end); but we bring with eagerness into the knowledge of your piety the divine working of heavenly matters accomplished in Jerusalem in the times of your God-loving majesty; not so that you may now come from ignorance into knowledge of God (for you are already teaching others through the things in which you are pious); but so that, the things which you knew, in these you may also be confirmed, and, having received the ancestral inheritance of the kingdom, having learned that you have been honored with greater heavenly crowns from God, you may both now give to God the King of all the fitting thanksgiving, and may be filled with greater courage against enemies, having understood in deed that your majesty is loved by God, through the things which he works wondrously in your time. For in the time of the most God-loving Constantine of blessed memory, your father, the saving wood of the cross was found in Jerusalem, the divine grace having granted to the one nobly seeking piety the finding of the hidden holy places.

pass_b_english: To Constantius Augustus, the emperor most God-loving and most pious, Cyril, bishop in Jerusalem, greetings in the Lord. These first fruits of letters I send from Jerusalem to your God-loving majesty—fitting for you to receive and for me to offer. They are not filled with flattering words, but they announce heavenly visions. They do not contain clever rhetorical persuasions of speech, but they bear witness to the truth of the holy Gospels' predictions through the outcome of events.

Others, for their part, often crown your honored head with what they have, bringing crowns inlaid with gold and adorned with brilliant stones. But we do not crown you with things from the earth—for gifts from the earth have the earth as their end. Rather, we eagerly bring to the knowledge of your piety a divine working of heavenly things accomplished in Jerusalem during the times of your God-loving reign. Not so that you might now pass from ignorance into knowledge of God—for you are already teaching others through your piety—but so that what you already knew you might also have confirmed, and so that, having received the ancestral inheritance of the kingdom, you might learn that you have been honored with greater heavenly crowns from God, and might now render fitting thanksgiving to God the King of all, and might be filled with greater courage against your enemies, understanding in deed that your reign is loved by God through the wonders He works in your time.

For in the time of Constantine, your father, most God-loving and of blessed memory, the saving wood of the cross was found in Jerusalem, when divine grace granted to the one who nobly sought piety the finding of the hidden holy places.

problems.why: Reverses agency; source says he loves God, not that God loves him.
problems.ruling: θεοφιλεστάτῳ = 'most God-loving' (active), not 'most beloved of God' (passive); agency reversed.

last_rejected.ruling: τῷ καλῶς ζητοῦντι = to the one who seeks piety well/rightly; 'nobly' is a stylistic nuance, not a substantive mistranslation.
